extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of philosophy and logic
extracted.subtask_description: Extracts and evaluates the standards Mill discusses for accepting beliefs and assessing deductive and inductive reasoning — e.g., mathematical certainty, the role of assumptions in deduction, Spencer's 'inconceivableness' test, and uniformity of experience. Useful for judging when a proposition is warranted.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mathematical certainty limited to pure Number
rubrics_metrics.description: What is commonly called mathematical certainty (unconditional truth and perfect accuracy) is not an attribute of all mathematical truths, but of those only which relate to pure Number, as distinguished from Quantity in the more enlarged sense; and only so long as we abstain from supposing that the numbers are a precise index to actual quantities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mill emphasizes that arithmetic conclusions are exactly true only when they concern number alone; when number is taken as an index to real-world quantities (weights, lengths, horse-power, etc.) an additional hypothesis (e.g., equality of units) is implied and may be false. Examples: one pound troy vs one pound avoirdupois; measured miles differing. Use this to judge claims of 'mathematical certainty' — check whether the claim depends on empirical equality of units.

rubrics_metrics.name: Deductive sciences are hypothetical and must be tested for assumption-truth
rubrics_metrics.description: The method of all Deductive Sciences is hypothetical: they proceed by tracing the consequences of certain assumptions, leaving for separate consideration whether the assumptions are true or not, and if not exactly true, whether they are a sufficiently near approximation to the truth.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating deductive arguments, separate (1) the derivation of consequences from assumptions (demonstrative science) and (2) the empirical question whether the assumptions hold for the case at hand. The latter generally requires observation and may vary case-by-case; precompute inferences from assumptions so that when instances arise you only test the fit of assumptions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Arithmetic presupposes equality of units (the hidden hypothesis 1=1)
rubrics_metrics.description: In all propositions concerning numbers, a condition is implied, without which none of them would be true; and that condition is an assumption which may be false — that 1=1; that all the numbers are numbers of the same or of equal units.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this as a checklist when applying arithmetic to empirical quantities: confirm units are equivalent (weights, measures, strengths) before inferring quantitative equalities. Anti-pattern: applying raw arithmetic across heterogeneous units leads to false conclusions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Certainty of inference is conditional on truth of premises
rubrics_metrics.description: The certainty usually ascribed to the conclusions of geometry, and even to those of mechanics, is nothing whatever but certainty of inference. We can have full assurance of particular results under particular suppositions, but we can not have the same assurance that these suppositions are accurately true.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When appraising 'certain' conclusions, distinguish certainty of logical consequence from certainty that premises match reality. Always ask: are the premises true or close enough? Do not conflate deductive validity with empirical truth.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reductio ad absurdum as a method to show false assumptions
rubrics_metrics.description: Sometimes the consequences of false assumptions are knowingly deduced for the purpose of showing the falsity of the assumption; which is called a reductio ad absurdum.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat proofs by contradiction as a legitimate tool to refute premises: derive consequences from the assumption and show they conflict with known facts or produce contradiction, thereby rejecting the assumption. Note Mill's account of how reductio functions in argumentation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inconceivableness of negation as a proposed universal test of truth (Spencer's doctrine)
rubrics_metrics.description: Mr. Spencer's doctrine: whenever any fact or proposition is invariably believed (believed by all persons and by oneself at all times), it is entitled to be received as one of the primitive truths; and the criterion by which we decide whether anything is invariably believed is our inability to conceive its negation — 'the inconceivableness of its negation is the test by which we ascertain whether a given belief invariably exists.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is the target criterion under critique. When applying this test, check whether 'inconceivableness' is intended as inability to form an idea or inability to sustain belief. Mill examines both the positive (it represents aggregate past experience) and negative (no stronger evidence exists) arguments given for this test. Use Mill's criticisms before accepting inconceivableness as decisive.

rubrics_metrics.name: Uniformity of past experience as a (separate) criterion for belief
rubrics_metrics.description: Every such belief [whose negation is inconceivable] represents the aggregate of all past experience. The inconceivableness of a thing implies that it is wholly at variance with the register of experience. Further: 'if, after an immense accumulation of experiences, there remain beliefs of which the negations are still inconceivable, most, if not all of them, must correspond to universal objective facts.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mill argues that uniformity of experience is the real evidential ground and should be appealed to directly rather than via inconceivableness. Examples given: metals sinking in water vs 'all swans are white' (invalidated by new evidence). When judging a belief, assess the scope and pervasiveness of supporting experience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inconceivableness can be misleading (tradition, association, imagination)
rubrics_metrics.description: Inconceivableness is not a test of experience because numerous causes (tradition, strong associations, familiar modes of production) can make alternatives appear inconceivable; inconceivableness may dominate and override actual experience.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Watch for anti-patterns where cultural tradition, associative habits, or imaginative familiarity make a negation seem impossible though experience does not support it. Examples: Cartesians' insistence on contact as the only cause of motion; sunrise/sunset intuitive conception vs scientific explanation. Do not accept 'inconceivableness' claims without checking for such confounders.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish 'unimaginable' (idea-forming) from 'unbelievable' (holding belief) when using 'inconceivable'
rubrics_metrics.description: Two meanings of 'inconceivable': inability to form an idea (unimaginable) vs inability to form or get rid of a belief (unbelievable). The argument from inconceivableness often equivocates between these senses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Require conceptual precision: clarify whether a claim's negation cannot be conceived imaginatively, or cannot be believed. Mill stresses this distinction with examples (antipodes — imaginable but unbelievable; end to extension — unimaginable). Failure to distinguish these leads to faulty inferences about truth.

rubrics_metrics.name: The Universal Postulate underpinning ratiocination ('whatever has a mark, has what it is a mark of')
rubrics_metrics.description: Mill identifies the fundamental maxim of ratiocination: that whatever has a mark, has what it is a mark of; or in universal propositions, that whatever is a mark of anything is a mark of whatever else that thing is a mark of. This axiom is what reasoning ultimately rests upon and is often renewed at each inferential step according to Spencer.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating syllogistic or chain reasoning, inspect reliance on this axiom. Mill disputes Spencer's claim that repetition of the postulate at each step multiplies the chance of error — the same axiom repeated doesn't create independent chances of error. Still, one should examine and justify this foundational maxim when assessing the validity of ratiocination.

rubrics_metrics.name: Number of inferential steps does not necessarily multiply error if no new premises introduced
rubrics_metrics.description: If the same axiom is assumed at each step, repetition of the assumption does not weaken the force of the argument; if it is true once, it is true every time. The number of steps does not subtract from reliableness provided no new premises of uncertain character are introduced.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this principle when assessing long deductive chains: long chains are not inherently less reliable than short ones so long as they introduce no additional questionable premises. Focus critique on premises added during the chain rather than on chain length alone.

rubrics_metrics.name: Belief invariability must be genuinely universal to serve as proof
rubrics_metrics.description: Mr. Spencer's idea that beliefs 'invariably exist' can be false: there have been persons who do not believe the reality of an external world, space, time, etc. The negations of these alleged invariable beliefs are not unbelievable because they are believed by some.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Before treating 'invariability of belief' as evidence, verify its factual universality across persons and time. Temporary or culturally variable belief-states disqualify the claim of invariability; psychological pressure or momentary credences do not equal permanent belief. Mill's critique is to demand empirical verification of invariability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer grounding belief on uniform experience rather than on inconceivableness alone
rubrics_metrics.description: Even if inconceivableness represents the net result of past experience, the actual uniformity of experience is the real evidence and directly accessible; we should state and weigh the uniformity of experience openly when using it as justification.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When justifying a conclusion, cite the extent and nature of prior experience supporting it instead of appealing indirectly to the impossibility of conceiving the contrary. Mill recommends assessing how strong the uniformity is (pervasive vs occasional) and the degree of evidential weight it supplies (strong, weak, negligible).
